extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, historians, and statesmen
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical criteria for forming and preserving stable republican governments, managing factions, and acquiring legitimate popular support. Drawn from Machiavellian reflections and historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution grounded in human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution formed upon the nature of man, and providing against his discontented temper, instead of trusting to what is not in him (his moderation and contentment in power), may preserve union, harmony, and tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions that assume self-interest and propensity to discontent; do not rely on the innate moderation or virtue of rulers or assemblies to maintain unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (legislative, executive, judicial)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is easily done by distinct and independent legislative, executive, and judicial powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create institutional independence among branches to check ambitions and prevent concentration of power. The text explicitly recommends distinct independent powers as a primary safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral / two councils in the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide ... two councils in the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a bicameral or dual-council legislative structure to moderate disagreements and prevent single-assembly dominance that can produce instability or party capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent feuds from growing into factions/parties
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible ... entirely to prevent feuds and animosities in [a republic]; it ought to be his chief care to provide against their growing up into factions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that disputes will arise but build procedural and institutional barriers (e.g., separation of powers, multiple councils) to stop personal or sectional animosities from crystallizing into organized factions that threaten the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some divisions are beneficial; not all divisions must be suppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences and divisions for the most part are prejudicial to republics; and yet it is certain there are some that are of service to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish harmful factionalism from constructive competition and institutionalized division (checks and balances). Allow and channel certain divisions so they produce beneficial emulation rather than destructive conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trust a single assembly or single ruler
rubrics_metrics.description: Republics that trust the content of one or two assemblies are as credulous, ignorant, and servile, as nations that trust the moderation of a single man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concentrating authority in one or a small number of assemblies or individuals; disperse power to reduce vulnerability to corruption, capture, or poor judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two roads to popularity: public office vs private beneficence
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two roads to popularity in such states, the one through public stations, the other through private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and evaluate sources of political popularity: (a) achievements in public office (victories, wise embassies, sound counsel) and (b) private acts (beneficence, protecting citizens from magistrates, financial largesse, entertainments). The former is more creditable to the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer popularity earned by public merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The reputation that is acquired the other way [through public service] is of credit and advantage to it, when not made a tool to party and faction, because it conduces to the good of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and reward public-spirited service (successful governance, military/political successes, wise counsel). Such reputation tends to benefit the commonwealth and is less likely to be exploited for private ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn against popularity gained via private largesse and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: This manner of proceeding [beneficence, supplying money, promoting to honours, entertaining the people with plays and spectacles, and distributing largesses] procures followers and partisans: and as popularity thus obtained is dangerous to the state, because it is commonly applied to serve private and self-interested views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat gifts, patronage, entertainments, and indiscriminate promotion with caution: though they win followers, they risk creating clientelistic factions and undermining public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster healthy emulation among citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: And though emulation and envy will always spring up even among citizens of the latter sort, yet, as they have no partisans that follow them for their own private ends, they cannot hurt the commonwealth; on the contrary, they must of necessity be of service to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote rivalry based on merit (public achievements) rather than partisan allegiance; healthy competition incentivizes public virtue and service without producing dangerous party machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers should seek to be honoured and beloved; distrust nobles/multitude when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Such examples ought to be warnings to princes, to reign in such a manner as to make themselves honoured and beloved by their subjects; and to others, against trusting to nobles or the multitude, except in a very good cause; for though these may be discontented to the last degree, they will seldom stir a foot to their assistance in distress or danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise rule that builds popular esteem (honor and affection), but be politically wary of relying on nobles or crowds for crucial support—use their aid only when causes are sound and trustworthy.
